MASTER SUBSCRIPTION AGREEMENT AMENDMENT AND SLA SCHEDULE
Between Thornfield Logistics, Inc. ("Customer") and Meridian Cloud Systems, Inc. ("Provider")
Effective Date: February 1

BACKGROUND
Customer subscribes to Provider's fleet-tracking analytics platform under the base Master Subscription Agreement dated the prior year. This Amendment revises the pricing and service-level terms for the upcoming renewal term. An earlier draft of this Amendment, shared with Customer's procurement team on December 3, proposed capping annual renewal price increases at ten percent (10%). Customer's procurement team pushed back during negotiation, and the parties agreed to the five percent (5%) cap reflected in Section 2 below, which is the term that governs.

1. SUBSCRIPTION FEE
The annual subscription fee for the platform is $54,000, billed monthly at $4,500. This fee covers up to 200 tracked vehicles and standard reporting features, with additional vehicles billed separately under a supplemental schedule not otherwise addressed in this Amendment.

2. RENEWAL AND PRICE CAP
This Agreement renews automatically for successive one-year terms unless either party provides at least sixty (60) days' written notice of non-renewal before the end of the then-current term. Upon each renewal, Provider may increase the subscription fee by no more than five percent (5%) over the prior term's fee. The ten percent (10%) figure discussed in the December 3 draft does not appear anywhere in the final terms and was specifically rejected during negotiation.

3. SERVICE LEVEL AGREEMENT
Provider commits to 99.9% platform uptime, measured monthly, excluding scheduled maintenance windows announced at least 48 hours in advance. For each full 0.1 percentage point that measured uptime falls below 99.9% in a given month, Customer is entitled to a service credit equal to 5% of that month's subscription fee. Service credits in any single month are capped at 50% of that month's subscription fee, regardless of how far uptime fell below target.

4. CREDIT REQUEST PROCESS
Customer must request any service credit in writing within 30 days of the end of the affected billing month. Credits are applied to the following month's invoice and are Customer's sole and exclusive remedy for any uptime shortfall, except in the case of a shortfall caused by a security incident, which is addressed separately under Section 9 of the base Agreement. A late request forfeits the credit for that month only; it does not affect Customer's ability to request credits for future months.

5. AUGUST UPTIME INCIDENT
Provider's monthly uptime report for August showed measured uptime of 99.5%, following a five-hour outage caused by a failed database migration on August 14. This is 0.4 percentage points below the 99.9% target, corresponding to four full 0.1-point increments. Customer submitted a timely credit request on September 3, within the 30-day window.

6. HYPOTHETICAL SCENARIOS DISCUSSED DURING NEGOTIATION
During negotiation, the parties discussed, for illustration only and not as a real event, what credit would apply if uptime fell as low as 98.0% in some future month: nineteen full 0.1-point increments below target would calculate to well above the 50% cap, illustrating why Section 3's cap exists. No such low-uptime month has actually occurred under this Agreement to date; August's 99.5% is the only shortfall on record.

7. TERM AND TERMINATION FOR CONVENIENCE
Either party may terminate this Agreement for convenience with ninety (90) days' written notice, separate from the sixty-day non-renewal notice described in Section 2, which applies specifically to stopping an automatic renewal rather than ending an active term early.

8. GENERAL
This Amendment, together with the base Master Subscription Agreement, constitutes the entire agreement regarding these terms and supersedes the December 3 draft in its entirety.

SIGNATURES
For Thornfield Logistics, Inc.: Ottilie Brandt, Director of Procurement
For Meridian Cloud Systems, Inc.: Samir Kassab, VP Customer Success

MILBROOK ARTS COUNCIL
Minutes of the Annual Budget Meeting
Date: June 18 | Location: Milbrook City Hall, Room 204 | Recorded by: Felix Ndiaye, Council Clerk

ATTENDANCE
Present: Chairperson Ingrid Halvorsen, Vice Chair Marcus Oduya, Board Members Rosalind Kanu, Theo Marsh, and Priyanka Chatterjee. Staff: Executive Director Beatrice Adeyemi.

CALL TO ORDER
Chairperson Halvorsen called the meeting to order at 4:00 p.m. and confirmed the total operating budget for the coming fiscal year at $420,000, drawn from municipal allocation, a state arts grant, and private donations.

BUDGET DISCUSSION — PUBLIC MURAL PROGRAM
Executive Director Adeyemi opened by noting the Mural Program received $45,000 last fiscal year. Facing a projected shortfall in the state grant, staff's initial budget draft proposed cutting the program to $30,000, a reduction of one third, to help balance the overall budget. During the public comment period, eleven community members spoke in support of restoring Mural Program funding, citing three murals currently in progress that would be left unfinished at $30,000. After discussion, Theo Marsh moved to fund the Mural Program at $40,000 instead of the originally proposed $30,000, using savings identified elsewhere in the administrative budget. Priyanka Chatterjee seconded. The motion passed 4-1, with Rosalind Kanu opposed on the grounds that it did not fully restore the prior year's level. The final approved figure for the Mural Program is $40,000.

BUDGET DISCUSSION — YOUTH THEATER PROGRAM
The Youth Theater Program was maintained at its prior level, $60,000, with no proposed changes. Marcus Oduya moved to approve the Youth Theater Program budget as presented; Theo Marsh seconded. The motion passed 5-0.

NEW PROGRAM PROPOSAL — DIGITAL ARTS LAB
Beatrice Adeyemi presented a proposal to launch a new Digital Arts Lab offering, at a first-year cost of $25,000, to teach digital illustration and animation tools to teens. Board members were supportive of the concept but concerned about funding it in a year when the Mural Program itself needed supplemental savings to avoid a deeper cut. Rosalind Kanu moved to table the Digital Arts Lab proposal for reconsideration next fiscal year rather than fund it this year. The motion to table passed 5-0. The Digital Arts Lab was not funded this year.

REGIONAL CONTEXT
For context, Executive Director Adeyemi noted that the neighboring Thistle County Arts Board cut its comparable mural program by 50% last year due to a larger funding gap; Milbrook's situation, while tight, did not require cuts of that scale, and the board expressed hope that this year's restoration effort keeps Milbrook's program meaningfully ahead of that comparison. Board Member Marsh asked whether Milbrook's grant application for next year could specifically cite the mural program's community turnout numbers to strengthen the case for restoring full funding going forward; Adeyemi agreed to include that data in the application, due to the state arts office in October.

FUNDING SOURCES RECAP
Adeyemi reminded the board how the $420,000 total budget breaks down: $260,000 from municipal allocation, $110,000 from the state arts grant, and $50,000 from private donations and the spring gala. She noted the state grant portion is the piece under the most pressure next year, which is the underlying reason the Mural Program cut was proposed in the first place rather than being an isolated program-specific decision.

OTHER BUSINESS
The board approved routine renewal of the council's liability insurance policy at $8,200 for the year, consistent with last year's rate, without discussion. Ingrid Halvorsen reminded members that the fall gallery opening date will be finalized at the September meeting, and asked staff to circulate a one-page summary of tonight's budget decisions to all program grantees before that meeting.

ADJOURNMENT
Meeting adjourned at 5:35 p.m. Next meeting: September 10.

Minutes respectfully submitted by Felix Ndiaye, Council Clerk.

Customer: Colin Draper | Account: Residential Internet, 500 Mbps plan ($90/month) | Opened: Sept 11

[Sept 11, 08:30] Colin Draper (Customer): My internet was down for about 6 hours yesterday afternoon, from roughly 1pm to 7pm, which is a long time for a single outage in my experience. I work from home and had to reschedule two calls. Can I get a credit for this?

[Sept 11, 09:05] Internal note (Nora Lindqvist, Support Tier 1): Checking outage logs for Colin's service area (Zone 14) on Sept 10. Confirmed a fiber cut affected Zone 14 from 13:02 to 19:11, approximately 6 hours 9 minutes. Per Service Credit Policy SC-7: any single outage event lasting 4 or more consecutive hours qualifies the affected account for a flat $15 service credit, applied to the next invoice. This clearly qualifies given the roughly 6-hour duration.

[Sept 11, 09:20] Nora Lindqvist (Support): Hi Colin, sorry about the disruption. I confirmed an outage in your area from about 1:02pm to 7:11pm on Sept 10, which qualifies for our standard $15 service credit under policy SC-7. I've applied that to your account, you'll see it reflected on your next invoice.

[Sept 11, 09:32] Colin Draper (Customer): Thanks, appreciate the quick response. My neighbor mentioned she had a shorter outage too, does she get something as well?

[Sept 11, 09:50] Internal note (Nora Lindqvist): Checked the neighbor's account, a different household in the same Zone 14. Her service dropped from 1:02pm to approximately 4:00pm, about 3 hours, before her specific segment was rerouted ahead of the rest of the zone during repair. That's under the 4-hour qualifying threshold in SC-7, so her account does not qualify for the flat credit, even though it's the same underlying fiber cut.

[Sept 11, 10:05] Nora Lindqvist (Support): I checked, and her outage was closer to 3 hours since her segment was restored earlier during the repair. Since our policy requires at least 4 consecutive hours for the flat credit, her account wouldn't qualify this time, though I'd encourage her to reach out directly if she wants us to double check her specific timing.

[Sept 11, 10:10] Colin Draper (Customer): Got it, makes sense. Separate question: is this the same as the credit I got back in August? I thought that one was bigger.

[Sept 11, 10:25] Internal note (Nora Lindqvist): Checking history: in August, Colin's account received a $40 credit following a 10-hour regional outage, a separate, larger fiber cut affecting three zones on Aug 3. That was calculated under the escalated-outage tier of SC-7, which applies a larger credit for outages affecting multiple zones simultaneously and lasting 8 or more hours. That escalated tier does not apply here since Sept 10 affected only Zone 14 and lasted under 8 hours.

[Sept 11, 10:40] Nora Lindqvist (Support): Good memory. The August credit was larger because that outage affected multiple zones and lasted over 8 hours, which triggers a different, higher credit tier in our policy. Yesterday's outage was contained to one zone and under 8 hours, so it falls under the standard flat-credit tier at $15.

[Internal thread note, added Sept 12 by Colin Draper's account manager, Piotr Zielinski] For broader context: last quarter, a customer advocacy group proposed that Vesper prorate credits for every outage regardless of duration, down to the minute, rather than using threshold tiers. The policy team evaluated this in July and rejected it, citing the administrative cost of minute-level proration against the relatively small number of sub-4-hour outages reported. SC-7's threshold-based tiers remain the current policy.

Ticket status: Resolved — $15 credit applied.

THISTLEDOWN FOODS — PROCESSING PLANT INCIDENT REPORT
Facility: Millbrook Processing Plant | Report No. TF-INC-0512
Incident Date: November 2 | Report Date: November 9
Prepared by: Plant Operations (Lead: Callan Reid)

INCIDENT SUMMARY
On November 2, Freezer Storage Unit 7 lost effective temperature control beginning at approximately 7:00 a.m. and was not detected until a routine walk-through at 12:30 p.m., a gap of five and a half hours. By the time the issue was found, internal temperature had risen from the required -10°F to 19°F. All 3,200 pounds of frozen mixed vegetables stored in Unit 7 were deemed unsafe for sale under the plant's food-safety protocol and were discarded, a loss valued at $1.35 per pound, or $4,320 in inventory.

INITIAL HYPOTHESIS
Because the plant experienced a brief grid voltage fluctuation that morning, the initial on-call response assumed a power interruption might be responsible and checked whether the backup generator had failed to engage. Power logs reviewed during the investigation show the backup generator was not needed and never engaged, because grid power to the plant was continuous throughout the morning with only the brief fluctuation, which was well within normal tolerance and did not trip any protective relay. The backup generator itself was tested afterward and found fully operational. Power interruption is therefore ruled out as a cause.

ROOT CAUSE
Maintenance technicians traced the failure to a burned-out compressor relay specific to Unit 7's cooling system, which prevented the compressor from cycling on despite the control system correctly calling for cooling. The relay showed clear signs of thermal damage consistent with a slow internal failure rather than a sudden trip. This is unrelated to a separate incident eight months ago involving Unit 3, where a worn fan belt caused reduced airflow; that unit uses different cooling hardware entirely and its repair history has no bearing on this incident.

CONTRIBUTING FACTOR: ALARM THRESHOLD
Investigators found that Unit 7's temperature logs show a slow upward drift beginning around 7:00 a.m., reaching 0°F by 9:30 a.m. and continuing to climb from there. The automated deviation alarm for Unit 7 was configured to trigger only when temperature exceeded 10°F, a threshold set during initial installation and never revisited. Had the threshold been set closer to the -10°F target, staff would likely have been alerted more than two hours earlier than the 12:30 p.m. walk-through, potentially reducing or eliminating the product loss.

DISCUSSION OF RESPONSES
Plant Operations discussed installing a fully redundant backup compressor on every freezer unit facility-wide, at an estimated cost of $180,000 across all twelve units. Given the cost and the fact that this is the first compressor-relay failure of its kind in the facility's operating history, leadership decided not to pursue full redundancy this year; the proposal was deferred to next year's capital planning cycle for further evaluation rather than being adopted now.

ACTIONS ADOPTED
1. Replace the failed relay on Unit 7 and proactively inspect equivalent relays on all other units by November 16 (completed for Unit 7 immediately; other units on schedule).
2. Tighten the deviation alarm threshold on all freezer units from 10°F to 2°F above target, with SMS paging to the on-duty technician in addition to the existing dashboard alert (owner: Callan Reid, due November 12).
3. Increase walk-through frequency for all freezer units from once per six hours to once per two hours until the alarm threshold change is verified in production (owner: Shift Supervisors, effective immediately).

FINANCIAL IMPACT SUMMARY
Direct inventory loss: $4,320. No equipment damage beyond the single relay, which cost $340 to replace. No injuries occurred. No customer shipments were affected, since the discarded batch had not yet left the facility.

SIGN-OFF
Approved by Callan Reid, Plant Operations Lead, and countersigned by the Facility Director, November 9.

CEDARVALE RETAIL GROUP — INTERNAL CONTROLS AUDIT SUMMARY
Subject: Store-Level Cash Handling Review, Fiscal Q3
Prepared by: Internal Audit (Lead: Fatima Rashid)
Distribution: Audit Committee, Regional Managers
Date Issued: October 30

SCOPE AND METHODOLOGY
This review examined till-level cash variance, the difference between expected cash based on register transactions and actual counted cash, across four sampled stores over a rolling 30-day period in Q3, chosen to represent a range of store sizes and revenue tiers. Per Controls Policy CP-9, cumulative variance over the period is classified as follows: a net shortage exceeding $5,000 is a "significant deficiency," a net shortage between $1,000 and $5,000 is a "minor deficiency," and anything within plus or minus $1,000 is "satisfactory." A net overage is never classified as a deficiency regardless of size, though large overages are separately flagged for count-accuracy review.

FINDINGS BY STORE
Store #14 (Northgate location, annual revenue approximately $3.1M): cumulative 30-day cash variance of negative $10,200, averaging a shortage of roughly $340 per day. This substantially exceeds the $5,000 significant-deficiency threshold. The pattern of consistent small daily shortages, rather than one large one-time discrepancy, is consistent with the profile Internal Audit typically associates with skimming rather than simple counting error, though this report does not make a finding of intentional misconduct; that determination has been referred to Loss Prevention for further investigation.

Store #22 (Bayshore location, annual revenue approximately $1.4M): cumulative variance of negative $2,100 over the period. This falls within the "minor deficiency" band. Store management attributed this largely to two specific shifts with a trainee cashier and has already adjusted training procedures.

Store #08 (Elmridge location, annual revenue approximately $2.6M): cumulative variance of negative $650, within the satisfactory range.

Store #31 (Fairview location, annual revenue approximately $900K): cumulative variance of positive $300, also satisfactory; the small overage was not large enough to trigger separate count-accuracy review.

DISCUSSION
Only Store #14 is classified as a significant deficiency this quarter. Store #22's minor deficiency appears explained by a specific, already-addressed training gap rather than a systemic issue. Store #08 and Store #31, both satisfactory, required no further discussion. Internal Audit recommends Loss Prevention prioritize Store #14 for a focused investigation, including reviewing security footage covering the shifts with the largest daily shortages.

PRIOR AUDIT FOLLOW-UP
Last year's controls audit recommended requiring dual-employee cash counts at close for all store locations company-wide, regardless of size, to reduce variance risk broadly. The Audit Committee reviewed this in January and did not adopt it company-wide, citing labor-cost concerns for smaller stores where a second closing employee is not otherwise scheduled. Instead, the committee adopted a narrower version: mandatory dual-employee close counts only for stores with annual revenue over $2M. Under that adopted policy, Store #14 and Store #08 are both required to perform dual counts; Store #22 and Store #31 are not required to, given their revenue falls under the $2M line.

NOTE ON STORE #14 COMPLIANCE
Despite being subject to the dual-count requirement since February, Store #14's variance this quarter suggests either inconsistent compliance with the dual-count procedure or that dual counts alone are insufficient to catch the pattern observed; Internal Audit recommends Loss Prevention's investigation also verify whether dual counts were actually being performed as required during the sampled period.

RECOMMENDATIONS
1. Loss Prevention to investigate Store #14 immediately, including footage review.
2. Verify actual dual-count compliance at Store #14 given the policy has been in effect since February.
3. Continue the revenue-based dual-count policy as adopted; no change recommended to the $2M threshold at this time.
4. Repeat this sampling methodology next quarter across the same four stores plus two additional locations chosen at random, to broaden coverage gradually without expanding scope too quickly.

Signed, Fatima Rashid, Lead Auditor, Internal Audit.

SUPPLY AGREEMENT
Between Anchorline Shipping, Inc. ("Buyer") and Redgate Components, Ltd. ("Supplier")
Effective Date: January 10

RECITALS
Supplier manufactures marine hardware components. Buyer purchases components under individual purchase orders issued against this master Supply Agreement. An earlier draft circulated December 2 proposed a late-delivery penalty of two percent (2%) of order value per week late. That draft term is superseded by Section 4 below, following further negotiation.

1. ORDERS AND PRICING
Each purchase order ("PO") issued by Buyer and accepted by Supplier is governed by the pricing and quantities stated on the PO and the general terms of this Agreement.

2. DELIVERY
Supplier shall deliver ordered components by the delivery date stated on each PO. Time is of the essence except as modified by Section 5 (Force Majeure).

3. INSPECTION
Buyer has 10 business days after delivery to inspect and reject non-conforming goods. Goods not rejected in writing within that window are deemed accepted, without prejudice to any separate warranty claim discovered later through normal use.

3A. WARRANTY
Supplier warrants that all components will be free from material defects for eighteen (18) months from delivery. This warranty is separate from, and not affected by, any late-delivery penalty credited under Section 4; a component can be both delivered late and warranted normally, with each remedy assessed independently of the other.

4. LATE DELIVERY PENALTY
If Supplier delivers a PO after its stated delivery date for reasons other than Force Majeure under Section 5, Supplier shall credit Buyer a late-delivery penalty equal to one and one-half percent (1.5%) of that PO's total order value for each full week of delay, prorated for partial weeks, up to a maximum penalty of ten percent (10%) of that PO's order value. The 2% figure discussed in the December 2 draft was rejected during negotiation and does not apply to any PO under this Agreement.

5. FORCE MAJEURE
Neither party is liable for delay caused by events beyond its reasonable control, including natural disasters, war, and labor strikes affecting a party's suppliers or transportation providers, provided the delayed party gives notice within 5 business days of learning of the event and uses reasonable efforts to mitigate the delay. A delay excused under this Section is not subject to the penalty in Section 4.

6. PO-2291 DELIVERY RECORD
PO-2291, order value $200,000, had a stated delivery date of March 1. Actual delivery occurred March 22, three weeks (21 days) after the stated date. Supplier did not claim Force Majeure for this delay; internal correspondence attached to the PO file attributes the delay to a supplier-side production scheduling error, unrelated to any qualifying event under Section 5.

7. PO-2150 DELIVERY RECORD (FOR COMPARISON)
PO-2150, order value $140,000, had a stated delivery date of the prior November 5 and was actually delivered December 10, five weeks (35 days) late. Supplier gave timely notice of a dockworkers' strike affecting the port used for this shipment, documented in a notice dated November 8, within the 5-business-day window required by Section 5. Buyer's contract administrator confirmed this qualifies as Force Majeure. No late-delivery penalty applies to PO-2150 notwithstanding its longer delay, because the delay is excused under Section 5.

8. PAYMENT
Buyer pays each PO's invoice within 45 days of delivery, net of any penalty credit due under Section 4.

9. TERM
This Agreement continues for two years from the Effective Date, renewing automatically for one-year terms absent 90 days' notice of non-renewal from either party.

9A. NOTICES
All notices required under this Agreement, including Force Majeure notices under Section 5, must be sent by email to the designated contract administrator for each party, with a copy to that party's legal department, and are deemed given on the date sent if sent before 5:00 p.m. in the recipient's local time zone.

SIGNATURES
For Anchorline Shipping, Inc.: Wanjiru Kamau, VP Procurement
For Redgate Components, Ltd.: Declan Moriarty, Sales Director

Curriculum Committee Meeting Minutes
Date: February 20 | Recorded by: Soren Aabo, Committee Secretary

ATTENDANCE
Present: Chair Amara Chukwu, Professors Bram Vandermeer, Consuela Marques, Gideon Farley, Tariq Idris, Wanjiru Kamau. Absent: Professor Ingrid Halvorsen.

CALL TO ORDER
Chair Chukwu called the meeting to order at 2:00 p.m. to consider three curriculum proposals ahead of the March catalog deadline, noting the committee would need to finish all three items today to make the deadline.

PROPOSAL 1: CS 240 CREDIT HOUR CHANGE
Professor Vandermeer presented a proposal to increase CS 240 (Intro to Data Ethics) from 3 credit hours to 4 credit hours, adding a weekly 75-minute lab section focused on hands-on case-study analysis, in response to consistent student feedback that the current lecture-only format leaves insufficient time for applied discussion. The proposal includes a staffing plan using an existing teaching assistant line, so no new budget request accompanies it. After discussion about lab-space availability, which Facilities confirmed is available in the existing computing labs, Professor Marques moved to approve the credit-hour change effective the fall term. The motion passed 6-1, with Professor Farley opposed on the grounds that he would have preferred piloting the lab with one section before a full rollout.

PROPOSAL 2: CS 240 CORE REQUIREMENT STATUS
Separately, Professor Vandermeer also proposed making CS 240 a required core course for all Computer Science majors, rather than its current status as a popular but optional elective. Several members raised concern that adding another required course could push total core-requirement credit hours above the threshold the university's general education office prefers for major programs, potentially requiring a broader review. Professor Idris moved to table the core-requirement proposal pending a formal review by the Dean's office of the program's total required credit load, rather than deciding it today. The motion to table passed 5-2. CS 240 remains an elective for now; only its credit-hour value approved above changes this term.

PROPOSAL 3: CS 310 RETIREMENT
Professor Kamau proposed retiring CS 310 (Legacy Systems Programming), citing enrollment that has fallen below 8 students in each of the last three offerings and a curriculum that has not been substantively updated in nine years. The committee agreed the course no longer serves a clear need given that its content is now partially covered in an updated CS 260. Professor Farley moved to approve retiring CS 310, with one final offering in the coming fall term for students who need it to graduate, after which it will be removed from the catalog. The motion passed 7-0.

DISCUSSION: PRIOR YEAR PRECEDENT
Chair Chukwu reminded the committee of a similar-sounding proposal from last year, in which the Mathematics department requested increasing CS 150 (Intro to Programming, a course outside this committee's own department but reviewed jointly) from 4 to 5 credit hours. That proposal was rejected by the joint committee at the time, specifically because the university's accreditor caps total first-year credit load and the increase would have pushed a common first-year schedule over that cap. Chair Chukwu noted CS 240's approved change this year does not raise the same concern, since data ethics is typically taken in the second year, when schedules have more room under the cap.

OTHER BUSINESS
Professor Marques asked whether the CS 240 lab sections would be ready in time for fall registration, which opens April 1. Professor Vandermeer confirmed lab scheduling would be finalized by March 15, ahead of registration, and agreed to report back to the committee if that timeline slips.

ADJOURNMENT
Meeting adjourned at 3:15 p.m. Next meeting: April 10.

Minutes submitted by Soren Aabo, Committee Secretary.

MARROW BAY CREDIT UNION — SECURITY INCIDENT REPORT
Incident Reference: SEC-0091 | Classification: Contained, no confirmed unauthorized access
Prepared by: IT Security (Lead: Nora Lindqvist) | Report Date: May 6

SUMMARY
On April 29, a phishing email impersonating the credit union's IT helpdesk was sent to approximately 340 employees, asking recipients to "verify their password" through a fraudulent login page mimicking the internal email portal. The campaign was detected the same afternoon when three employees independently reported the email as suspicious.

SCOPE OF EMPLOYEE INTERACTION
Of the 340 recipients, email gateway logs and employee interviews establish the following: 3 employees reported the email without clicking any link, consistent with security awareness training. 1 employee, Selin Aydin (Operations), clicked the link, saw the fraudulent login page, became suspicious of the page's appearance, and closed the browser tab without entering any credentials. 1 employee, Emeka Uzo (Marketing), clicked the link and entered his network username and password into the fraudulent page. No other employees are confirmed to have interacted with the link based on available logs.

WHAT HAPPENED AFTER CREDENTIAL ENTRY
The attacker attempted to use Emeka Uzo's captured credentials to log into the credit union's email and single-sign-on portal at 2:14 p.m. on April 29, roughly eleven minutes after the phishing email was sent. Because multi-factor authentication is required for all portal logins, the attacker was prompted for a second factor and made three unsuccessful attempts, guessing or attempting to bypass the MFA challenge, before the account was automatically locked per policy after three failed MFA attempts. The attacker did not gain access to Emeka's account, the email system, or any other system. Critically, the core banking platform is on a fully separate authentication system that does not accept single-sign-on credentials at all, so even a successful email-account compromise would not by itself have provided any path to core banking systems; no core banking system was touched, queried, or accessed at any point during this incident.

REMEDIATION TAKEN
Emeka Uzo's password was reset and his account was reviewed for any suspicious activity prior to the incident; none was found. The phishing sender domain was blocked at the email gateway. All-staff communication was sent April 30 reminding employees how to report suspicious emails, and thanking the three employees who reported the campaign promptly without naming them individually.

DISCUSSION OF PROPOSED RESPONSES
IT Security discussed a proposal to disable all clickable links in external emails company-wide as a blanket measure. This was not adopted; leadership determined it would significantly disrupt legitimate business communication with vendors and members, and that the existing combination of email filtering, security awareness training, and mandatory MFA already prevented this incident from resulting in any actual compromise. Instead, the committee adopted a narrower measure: emails from newly-registered external domains, registered within the last 30 days, will now be automatically flagged with a warning banner, since the phishing domain used in this campaign had been registered only 6 days before the attack.

TRAINING FOLLOW-UP
Emeka Uzo and Selin Aydin were both enrolled in a supplemental phishing-awareness refresher, though Selin's participation is recognition-based rather than corrective, since she correctly avoided entering credentials once she saw the page.

CONCLUSION
This incident is classified as contained with no confirmed unauthorized access to any system. The combination of MFA and account lockout policy prevented the one instance of credential entry from resulting in an actual compromise, and the core banking system was never at risk given its separate authentication architecture. This report will be shared with the Board's Risk Committee at its next scheduled quarterly meeting as part of routine security reporting.

Approved by Nora Lindqvist, IT Security Lead, May 6.

VANTAGE ANALYTICS — DATA RETENTION COMPLIANCE AUDIT
Prepared by: Compliance Office (Lead: Zara Whitmore) | Report Date: July 22
Scope: Review of retention practices against Data Retention Policy DR-5 across four data categories

BACKGROUND
Policy DR-5 sets maximum retention periods by data category: customer support transcripts, 24 months from ticket closure; marketing email engagement logs, 12 months from send date; billing and invoicing records, 84 months (7 years), reflecting statutory recordkeeping requirements; and internal employee system-access logs, 6 months from log creation. This audit sampled each category's live storage systems to check actual retention against these limits.

FINDINGS: SUPPORT TRANSCRIPTS
The audit found that approximately 12,000 support transcripts, all originating from a legacy ticketing system decommissioned two years ago but never fully purged, were still present in cold storage. The oldest of these transcripts dated to 41 months before the audit date, 17 months past the 24-month policy limit. This is a non-compliant finding. Investigation traced the cause to the legacy system's automated purge job, which was disabled during the system's decommissioning process and never re-enabled or replaced with an equivalent process for the archived data.

FINDINGS: MARKETING EMAIL LOGS
Sampled marketing email engagement logs showed an average retention of 10 months, with the oldest sampled record at 11.5 months, both within the 12-month policy limit. This category is compliant.

FINDINGS: BILLING RECORDS
Billing and invoicing records were found retained consistently at the required 84-month, 7-year, period, with automated deletion confirmed working correctly on a sample of records that crossed the 7-year mark during the audit window. This category is compliant.

FINDINGS: EMPLOYEE ACCESS LOGS
Access logs from the primary authentication system were compliant, purging correctly at 6 months. However, one secondary system, a legacy VPN gateway still in limited use, was found retaining access logs for 9 months, 3 months past the policy limit, affecting a smaller volume of records than the transcript finding but still a non-compliant result for that specific system.

DISCUSSION
Two of the four categories reviewed show non-compliant retention: support transcripts, significantly over limit and large volume, and one secondary system's employee access logs, moderately over limit and smaller volume. Marketing email logs and billing records are both compliant. The Compliance Office notes that neither non-compliant finding appears to reflect a policy that is unclear or poorly designed; both trace back to an operational gap in enforcement rather than confusion about what DR-5 requires.

PROPOSAL CONSIDERED
During the audit debrief, one committee member proposed shortening the support-transcript retention period further, to 12 months instead of 24, to reduce future compliance risk. This was not adopted as a policy change; the Compliance Office noted 24 months already reflects a negotiated balance with the support team's need to reference prior tickets for repeat issues, and the actual problem here was a broken purge process, not a retention period that was set too long. Shortening the limit would not have prevented this specific failure, since the purge job was disabled entirely rather than running on a longer schedule.

REMEDIATION
1. Legacy ticketing system's archived transcripts to be purged of all records older than 24 months by August 15 (owner: IT Infrastructure).
2. Automated purge job to be re-enabled and verified monthly going forward for the legacy archive specifically (owner: IT Infrastructure).
3. VPN gateway access logs to be reconfigured to a 6-month automatic purge, matching the primary system, by August 1 (owner: Network Security).
4. No change to the 24-month support-transcript policy limit itself, per the discussion above.

SIGN-OFF
Reviewed and accepted by Zara Whitmore, Compliance Lead, and the VP of Engineering, July 22. A follow-up review of all four categories is scheduled for January to confirm the remediation items above were completed on schedule.

BELLHAVEN CO-OP BOARD — SPECIAL MEETING MINUTES
Date: March 4 | Location: Building Lobby Community Room | Recorded by: Keiko Sano

ATTENDANCE
Present: President Gideon Farley, Vice President Consuela Marques, Treasurer Wanjiru Kamau, Directors Tariq Idris and Amara Chukwu. 34 of 52 shareholders represented in person or by proxy, meeting quorum.

CALL TO ORDER
President Farley called the special meeting to order at 6:30 p.m. to address four items: elevator replacement funding, a subletting policy change, a proposed pet policy amendment, and roof deck renovation funding, noting a fifth informational item on maintenance fees would follow time permitting.

ITEM 1: ELEVATOR REPLACEMENT SPECIAL ASSESSMENT
Treasurer Kamau presented engineering findings that both building elevators, installed 28 years ago, require full replacement rather than further repair, at a total contracted cost of $728,000. After reviewing financing options, the board proposed a one-time special assessment of $2,800 per unit, 260 units, to fund the replacement without depleting the reserve fund needed for other planned work. Shareholder discussion raised concerns about the timing but no alternative funding proposal was offered. A vote was held: 29 in favor, 5 opposed. The special assessment passed, payable in three installments over the next twelve months.

ITEM 2: SUBLETTING POLICY CHANGE
Vice President Marques presented a proposed rule change limiting any single sublet arrangement to a maximum of 2 consecutive years, after which the shareholder must either return to occupying the unit or apply for a limited extension requiring board approval. The current policy has no maximum duration at all. After discussion about grandfathering current subletters, the board agreed existing sublets in progress would be grandfathered until their current lease term ends, with the 2-year cap applying to all sublets starting after today. The policy change passed 31-3.

ITEM 3: PET POLICY AMENDMENT
Director Idris presented a shareholder-requested amendment to raise the current 25-pound dog weight limit, allowing larger dogs with board approval on a case-by-case basis. Several shareholders spoke against the change, citing concerns raised after a prior incident with a larger dog in a common hallway two years ago. After discussion, President Farley called for a vote: 14 in favor, 20 opposed. The amendment did not pass; the existing 25-pound limit remains in place unchanged.

ITEM 4: ROOF DECK RENOVATION
Director Chukwu presented a proposal to renovate the roof deck common area, estimated at $45,000, to be funded entirely from the existing capital reserve fund without any additional assessment on shareholders, since the reserve fund's roof-deck line item already has sufficient balance for this scope. The board confirmed with the managing agent that this spending is within the reserve fund's existing allocation and does not require a shareholder vote under the co-op's bylaws for reserve-funded capital work under $50,000. The board approved proceeding with the renovation administratively.

ITEM 5: MONTHLY MAINTENANCE FEE
Treasurer Kamau raised, as an informational item rather than a vote, that next year's operating budget may require a maintenance fee increase, estimated at around 4%, but said the exact figure depends on utility contract renewals still being negotiated. No motion was made and no vote was held on any fee increase at this meeting; the topic was tabled for the annual budget meeting in the fall, when firmer numbers will be available.

CLOSING
President Farley thanked shareholders for attending and reminded them that installment payment details for the elevator assessment will be mailed within two weeks, and that the roof deck renovation timeline will be shared once the managing agent finalizes a contractor.

ADJOURNMENT
Meeting adjourned at 8:05 p.m. President Farley thanked the board members for preparing the agenda materials in advance, which he credited with keeping tonight's meeting under two hours despite covering five separate items.

Minutes respectfully submitted by Keiko Sano.
